en: I came, I saw, I conquered.
explain: Julius Caesar's famous report after a quick victory. All three verbs are perfect, 1st person singular: _-ī_. Notice _vēnī_ (from _veniō_), _vīdī_ (_videō_), _vīcī_ (_vincō_): the stems change in the perfect.
distractors: These are present tense: “I come, I see, I conquer”. The saying looks back: perfect _vēnī, vīdī, vīcī_.

explain: _carpe_ is the command to one person from _carpō_. _diem_ is the accusative singular of _diēs_ (day).
distractors: _carpite_ is to several people. To one person: _carpe_.
_diēs_ is plural (“days”). The saying is singular: _diem_.

explain: _tempus_ (time) is a neuter noun with a nominative that looks like an accusative. _fugit_ means “flees, flies”, and agrees with it: 3rd person singular.
distractors: _tempora_ is plural (“times”). The saying is singular: _tempus fugit_.

explain: A real warning on Roman doorways. _cavē_ is the command to one person, and _cavēre_ takes the accusative: _canem_.
distractors: _cavēte_ is to several people. To one person: _cavē_.
_canis_ is nominative. After _cavē_ use the accusative: _canem_.

explain: A favorite motto of the emperor Augustus. _festīnā_ is the command to one person from _festīnō_, and _lentē_ is an adverb, so it never changes.
distractors: _festīnāte_ is to several people. To one person: _festīnā_.

explain: When the subject is an infinitive (_errāre_, “to err”), the adjective is neuter: _hūmānum_. Latin treats “to err” as a thing, neuter singular.
distractors: _hūmānus_ is masculine. An infinitive subject takes the neuter: _hūmānum_.
_errō_ is “I err”. “To err” is the infinitive: _errāre_.
_errāmus_ is “we err”. “To err” is the infinitive: _errāre_.

en: Art is long, life is short.
explain: Both nouns are feminine, so _longa_ goes with _ars_ and _brevis_ with _vīta_. _brevis_ is a 3rd-declension adjective: the same form for masculine and feminine.
distractors: _ars_ is feminine, so the adjective is _longa_.

explain: _fortūna_ is the subject (nominative), and _iuvat_ (helps) agrees with it. _audācēs_ is accusative plural, “the bold”, the ones who are helped. In Latin, _iuvō_ takes the accusative.
distractors: _fortūna_ is singular, so the verb is _iuvat_.

en: We learn not for school but for life.
explain: _scholae_ and _vītae_ are datives: “for school, for life”. _nōn … sed_ = not … but. _discimus_ is “we learn”.
distractors: “For” (the purpose or beneficiary) is the dative: _scholae_ and _vītae_.

en: If you want peace, prepare for war.
explain: _sī_ = if, _vīs_ = you want. _pācem_ is the accusative of _pāx_ (the thing wanted). _parā_ is the command to one person.
distractors: _parāte_ is to several people. To one person: _parā_.

explain: Two commands to one person: _dīvide_ (from _dīvidō_) and _imperā_ (from _imperō_). Third-conjugation commands end in _-e_; first-conjugation ones in _-ā_.
distractors: These are “he divides and rules”. The saying is a command: _dīvide et imperā_.
These are for several people. To one person: _dīvide et imperā_.
These are “I divide and rule”. The saying is a command: _dīvide et imperā_.

en: A healthy mind in a healthy body.
explain: _mēns_ is feminine, so _sāna_. _corpus_ is neuter and here ablative after _in_: _corpore_, so the adjective is _sānō_ too.
